title: TypeScript: why, setup and basic types
goal: Set up TypeScript, annotate basic types, and let the compiler catch mistakes before you run code.

concepts: What TypeScript adds: types checked at compile time, removed at runtime
Installing: npm i -D typescript tsx; npx tsc --init; strict mode
Basic types: string, number, boolean, arrays (number[]), tuples, null/undefined
Type inference: you don't annotate everything
any vs unknown: why any switches checking off
Running TS: tsc to type-check/compile, tsx to run directly

build.task: In day55/, run npm init -y, npm i -D typescript tsx, and npx tsc --init (keep "strict": true). Convert your Day 28 utils (capitalize, isValidEmail, clamp, randomInt, countVowels) and grades functions to utils.ts and grades.ts with parameter and return types. Add a scripts entry "check": "tsc --noEmit". Then write mistakes.ts with 6 deliberate type errors (wrong argument type, missing argument, calling a method that doesn't exist, possibly-undefined value, etc.); paste each compiler error as a comment and explain it in your own words; then comment the mistakes out so npm run check passes.
acceptance: tsconfig.json has strict: true
utils.ts and grades.ts have typed parameters and return types; no any
npm run check passes with zero errors
mistakes.ts documents 6 different compiler errors with explanations
npx tsx grades.ts runs and your checks pass

hints: Annotate parameters and return types for exported functions: function clamp(n: number, min: number, max: number): number { ... }. Let TS infer local variables.
If TS says 'Object is possibly undefined', it's telling you about a real case you haven't handled. Handle it; don't silence it.
VS Code shows TS errors as red squiggles. Hover to read the message, and read it slowly: the last line is usually the most useful.

explainBack.q: Pick one compiler error from mistakes.ts. Explain what bug it would have caused at runtime.
lookFor: names their error
describes the real runtime failure (undefined, NaN, crash)
caught before running

explainBack.q: What's the difference between any and unknown?
lookFor: any disables type checking
unknown requires narrowing before use
unknown is the safe choice for untrusted data

lastHintExplanation: TypeScript checks types while you write and compile, then strips them so the output is plain JavaScript. any turns checking off for that value, so mistakes slip through. unknown accepts any value but makes you check its type (narrow it) before using it, which makes it the safe type for untrusted data like JSON.

predict.q: let x = 5; x = 'five'; What does TypeScript do?
options: Error: string not assignable to number
predict.why: x is inferred as number from its initial value.

predict.q: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript. At runtime, does the browser check your types?
predict.why: Types exist only at compile time.

title: Interfaces, type aliases, unions and literal types
goal: Describe the shape of your data precisely so the compiler stops whole classes of bugs.

concepts: Object types with interface and type
Optional (?) and readonly properties
Union types: string | number; literal types: 'pending' | 'done'
Discriminated unions: { kind: 'card' ... } | { kind: 'upi' ... }
Intersection types (A & B) and extending interfaces
Index signatures and Record<string, number>

build.task: In day56/, model an online order system in types.ts: Customer, Address, Product (readonly id), CartItem, Order with status as a union of literal types ('placed' | 'packed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled'), and Payment as a discriminated union of upi { upiId }, card { last4, network }, and cod { }. In orders.ts write: orderTotal(order), describePayment(payment) using a switch on kind with an exhaustive never check, canCancel(order), and nextStatus(status). Create 3 sample orders and print summaries. Run npm run check.
acceptance: Status and payment kinds use literal unions, not plain string
Payment is a discriminated union; describePayment narrows correctly
Exhaustive check: adding a new payment kind causes a compile error in describePayment
Product id is readonly (assignment is a compile error)
Optional fields used where data may be missing (e.g. address line 2)
npm run check passes; sample output printed with tsx

hints: type Payment = { kind: 'upi'; upiId: string } | { kind: 'card'; last4: string; network: 'visa' | 'mastercard' | 'rupay' } | { kind: 'cod' };
Exhaustive check: in the switch's default: const _exhaustive: never = payment; return _exhaustive;. If a case is missing, TypeScript errors there.
interface vs type: either works for objects. Use type for unions; use interface when you want to extend object shapes.

explainBack.q: Explain how TypeScript knows payment.upiId exists inside case 'upi'.
lookFor: discriminant property kind
narrowing by checking the literal value
only the upi member has upiId

explainBack.q: What does the never check protect you from?
lookFor: forgetting to handle a new union member
compile error instead of runtime bug

lastHintExplanation: In a discriminated union, every member has a shared literal property (kind). Checking kind === 'upi' narrows the type to the upi member, so upiId becomes available. In the default branch every handled kind has been removed, so the value's type should be never. If someone adds a new payment kind and forgets a case, assigning it to never fails at compile time.

predict.why: Literal types are exact, including case.

title: Typed functions, narrowing and type guards
goal: Type functions fully, handle data of uncertain shape safely, and validate JSON at runtime.

concepts: Function types: (a: number) => string; optional and default parameters
Narrowing with typeof, instanceof, in, and truthiness
User-defined type guards: function isUser(x: unknown): x is User
Non-null assertion (!) and why to avoid it
Overloads (just know they exist)
Validating unknown JSON at runtime (TS types disappear!)

build.task: In day57/: (1) write formatValue(v: string | number | Date | null) that narrows each case. (2) Write a type guard isExpense(x: unknown): x is Expense and use it to safely load expenses from a JSON string, reporting invalid rows. (3) Do the same validation with zod (npm i zod): define an ExpenseSchema, infer the type with z.infer, and use safeParse. Compare both approaches in a comment. (4) Write a typed fetchJson<T>(url, guard) that returns T or throws if the guard fails, and use it with JSONPlaceholder /users.
acceptance: formatValue handles all 4 cases with no type errors and no any
isExpense checks every required field's type at runtime
zod schema with z.infer type; invalid rows reported with zod's error messages
fetchJson validates the response before returning it
No non-null assertions (!) in the code
npm run check passes

hints: Type guard skeleton: function isExpense(x: unknown): x is Expense { return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'amount' in x && typeof (x as any).amount === 'number' && ... }. (Using as any inside a guard is acceptable; avoid it elsewhere.)
zod: const ExpenseSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), amount: z.number().positive(), category: z.enum(['food', 'travel', 'bills']) }); type Expense = z.infer<typeof ExpenseSchema>;
res.json() returns Promise<any>. Assign it to unknown first so TypeScript forces you to validate.

explainBack.q: If TypeScript checks types, why do you still need runtime validation for JSON?
lookFor: types are erased at runtime
API/JSON data is outside the compiler's control
a type annotation is just a promise, not a check

explainBack.q: What does the 'x is Expense' return type do?
lookFor: tells TS that when it returns true, x is an Expense
narrows the type in the calling code

lastHintExplanation: TypeScript only checks code it compiles; data arriving at runtime (JSON, APIs, localStorage) has no types until you check it. Annotating it as Expense is just a claim. A type guard (x is Expense) or a zod schema checks the real values, and when it passes, TypeScript narrows the type in your code.

predict.q: const data = JSON.parse('{"age":"20"}') as { age: number }; console.log(data.age + 1)
predict.why: as doesn't convert anything; age is still the string '20' at runtime, so + concatenates.

title: Generics and utility types
goal: Write reusable, type-safe functions and types with generics, and use the built-in utility types.

concepts: Generic functions: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined
Generic constraints: <T extends { id: string }>
Generic types and interfaces: ApiResponse<T>
Utility types: Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly, ReturnType
keyof and indexed access types: T[K]
as const for literal tuples and objects

build.task: In day58/, write a typed generic toolkit with tests: groupBy<T, K extends string>(items, keyFn): Record<K, T[]>; uniqueBy<T>(items, keyFn); sortBy<T>(items, key: keyof T, dir); pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items, key): T[K][]; and a generic class Repository<T extends { id: string }> with add, update(id, changes: Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>>), remove, findById, and all(). Use it for two different types (Expense and Note) to show it's reusable. Write 12+ checks.
acceptance: All functions are generic and fully typed; no any
pluck's return type is inferred correctly (hover shows e.g. number[])
Repository.update accepts Partial changes and can't change id (compile error if tried)
Repository used with two different types
12+ passing checks; npm run check passes

hints: pluck: function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][] { return items.map(i => i[key]); }
update(id: string, changes: Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>>): T | undefined — Omit removes id, Partial makes the rest optional.
If you're tempted to write any, try a generic parameter or unknown first.

explainBack.q: Explain what K extends keyof T means in pluck, and what it prevents.
lookFor: K must be one of T's property names
prevents plucking a non-existent key
return type T[K][] matches the property type

explainBack.q: Explain Partial<Omit<T, 'id'>> in your own words.
lookFor: remove id from T
make remaining fields optional
so update can change some fields but never id

lastHintExplanation: Generics let a function work for many types while keeping the exact type. In pluck, K extends keyof T restricts the key to real property names of T, and T[K] is that property's type, so pluck(expenses, 'amount') returns number[]. Omit<T, 'id'> removes id, and Partial makes the remaining fields optional.

predict.q: function id<T>(x: T): T { return x } const r = id(['a', 'b']); What is the type of r?
predict.why: T is inferred from the argument as string[].

Optional properties must be handled before use
as casts don't convert or check anything
Fixing errors vs silencing them (any, !, @ts-ignore)
